items.q: (A) No sooner the bell had rung than the students (B) poured out of the classroom, (C) leaving behind a trail of (D) crumpled worksheets and pencil shavings.
options: No sooner the bell had rung
items.correction: No sooner had the bell rung
items.explanation: A sentence opening with the negative adverbial No sooner requires subject–auxiliary inversion: No sooner had the bell rung than…

items.q: The organising committee (A) has recommended that every athlete (B) submits a medical certificate (C) before competing in (D) the regional championships next spring.
items.explanation: After recommend that, the verb takes the present subjunctive (base form, no -s): that every athlete submit a certificate.

items.q: (A) After finishing the chemistry experiment, (B) the results were recorded by the students (C) in their notebooks (D) before the lesson ended.
options: the results were recorded by the students
items.explanation: A dangling modifier: the participle clause After finishing must describe the subject of the main clause, and the results did not finish anything — the students did.

items.q: Tom (A) would not be sitting on the bench today, (B) instead of leading the team out, (C) if he listened to his coach's advice (D) at the start of the season.
options: would not be sitting on the bench today
instead of leading the team out
if he listened to his coach's advice
at the start of the season
items.correction: if he had listened to his coach's advice
items.explanation: This is a mixed conditional: a past cause (at the start of the season) with a present result needs if + past perfect, not the simple past.

items.q: Many elderly villagers (A) who remember the steam trains (B) wish that the authorities (C) had listened to their protests (D) and did not close the line.
options: and did not close the line
items.correction: and had not closed the line
items.explanation: A wish about the past takes the past perfect, and the second verb is coordinated with had listened, so it must also be past perfect: had not closed.

items.q: (A) What impressed the judges most were (B) the clarity of the argument, (C) not the sheer volume of evidence (D) the debaters had gathered.
options: What impressed the judges most were
not the sheer volume of evidence
items.correction: What impressed the judges most was
items.explanation: In a wh-cleft, the what-clause is a singular subject and the complement (the clarity) is singular too, so the verb must be was.

items.q: The lecturer gave us (A) a great deal of advice on referencing (B) but far fewer information (C) about how to structure (D) the literature review itself.
options: a great deal of advice on referencing
items.explanation: Information is uncountable, so it takes less; fewer is reserved for plural countable nouns.

items.q: The renovated library offers students (A) a quiet place to read, (B) fast internet access, and (C) to borrow books (D) from partner universities abroad.
items.explanation: Items in a list must be parallel: two noun phrases (a quiet place, fast internet access) cannot be followed by an infinitive, so the third item needs a noun head as well.

items.q: The geneticist (A) drew a sharp distinction between (B) correlation and causation, (C) warning the audience not to (D) jump into conclusions.
items.explanation: The fixed idiom is jump to conclusions (reach a judgement too quickly); jump into does not collocate with conclusions.

items.q: Only after (A) the last guest had left (B) the hosts realised (C) that the silver candlesticks (D) were missing from the mantelpiece.
items.explanation: When a sentence begins with Only after + clause, the main clause is inverted: Only after the last guest had left did the hosts realise…

items.q: (A) Not knew what to expect, the young reporter (B) approached the senator (C) with a list of questions (D) she had rehearsed all morning.
items.explanation: A participle clause giving the reason for the main action uses the -ing form, negated with not in front: Not knowing what to expect.

items.q: The union leaders (A) demanded that the factory owner (B) reinstate the dismissed workers (C) and that he pays them (D) for the weeks they had lost.
options: for the weeks they had lost
items.explanation: Both that-clauses depend on demanded, so both verbs take the subjunctive base form: that he reinstate… and that he pay them.

items.q: Professor Lam, (A) whom research on coral bleaching (B) has won several international awards, (C) will deliver the keynote speech (D) at the conference in Nha Trang.
options: at the conference in Nha Trang
items.explanation: The research belongs to the professor, so the relative clause needs the possessive relative whose; whom can only be an object, never a determiner before a noun.

items.q: (A) Attributing her success with the years (B) she spent listening to strangers' conversations, (C) the novelist rarely takes credit (D) for her own imagination.
options: Attributing her success with the years
she spent listening to strangers' conversations
items.correction: Attributing her success to the years
items.explanation: The verb pattern is attribute something to something; with is not a possible preposition after attribute.

items.q: Had the city council (A) approved the drainage scheme in 2019, (B) the low-lying streets (C) would not flood every time (D) it will rain heavily.
items.explanation: A time clause introduced by every time (like when or as soon as) takes the present simple, never will, even when the sentence refers to the future.

items.q: The selection committee (A) considered the second of the two bids (B) the most persuasive, (C) largely because it addressed (D) the long-term cost of maintenance.
options: considered the second of the two bids
items.explanation: When exactly two things are compared, English uses the comparative (the more persuasive); the superlative needs three or more.

items.q: The twins (A) argued with each other so fiercely (B) that neither of them (C) noticed the teacher standing (D) directly behind themselves.
options: argued with each other so fiercely
items.explanation: A reflexive pronoun is only used when the object is the same person as the subject of its own clause; here the subject of standing is the teacher, so the plain object pronoun them is needed.

items.q: By the time the rescue helicopter (A) reached the ridge, (B) the stranded climbers (C) have been without food for almost three days (D) and could barely stand.
options: have been without food for almost three days
items.correction: had been without food for almost three days
items.explanation: By the time + past simple marks a point in the past; a state that lasted up to that point takes the past perfect, not the present perfect.

items.q: It was (A) the captain's composure, (B) rather than any tactical brilliance, (C) what carried the team (D) through the closing minutes of the final.
options: through the closing minutes of the final
items.explanation: An it-cleft (It was X…) is completed by that (or who), never by what; what only opens a wh-cleft such as What carried the team was…

items.q: (A) Scarcely had the orchestra finished tuning up (B) than the lights failed, (C) plunging the entire concert hall (D) into total darkness.
options: Scarcely had the orchestra finished tuning up
items.explanation: Scarcely / Hardly / Barely … pair with when; only No sooner is followed by than.

items.q: The (A) rapid expansion of online learning (B) has raised serious questions about (C) the reliable of assessments (D) conducted at a distance.
items.explanation: After the and before of, a noun is required: the adjective reliable must be nominalised to reliability.

items.q: The guide (A) explained that the temple (B) had been built in the twelfth century and (C) asked us whether (D) had we visited the older shrine nearby.
options: had been built in the twelfth century
had we visited the older shrine nearby
items.correction: we had visited the older shrine nearby
items.explanation: A reported yes/no question keeps statement word order after whether: asked us whether we had visited, with no inversion.

items.q: The astronauts (A) spent six months aboard the station, (B) conducting experiments on (C) how the human body adapts to (D) the life without gravity.
options: spent six months aboard the station
how the human body adapts to
items.explanation: Life used in a general, abstract sense takes no article; the life would point to one specific, already identified life.

items.q: (A) A large amount of volunteers (B) turned up to clear the beach, (C) far more than the organisers (D) had anticipated.
options: turned up to clear the beach
items.explanation: Amount of goes with uncountable nouns; volunteers is plural countable, so the quantifier must be a large number of.

items.q: (A) To qualify for the scholarship, (B) an essay must be submitted by applicants (C) before the end of March, (D) along with two academic references.
options: an essay must be submitted by applicants
items.explanation: A dangling infinitive: the purpose clause To qualify must attach to the person who qualifies, so applicants, not the essay, must be the subject of the main clause.

items.q: (A) Under no circumstances students are allowed (B) to bring calculators into the hall (C) once the exam papers (D) have been distributed.
options: Under no circumstances students are allowed
to bring calculators into the hall
items.correction: Under no circumstances are students allowed
items.explanation: A fronted negative phrase such as Under no circumstances triggers inversion of the auxiliary and subject: Under no circumstances are students allowed…

items.q: My younger brother (A) keeps borrowing my headphones (B) without ever asking, (C) and I really wish he will (D) stop doing it.
options: and I really wish he will
items.correction: and I really wish he would
items.explanation: Wish about someone else's annoying behaviour or a hoped-for change takes would, never will: I wish he would stop.

items.q: (A) Been locked away for decades, the documents (B) were finally released to historians, (C) revealing how close (D) the two nations had come to war.
options: the two nations had come to war
items.correction: Having been locked away for decades
items.explanation: A bare past participle been cannot open a clause; a perfect passive participle clause needs Having been locked away (or simply Locked away).

items.q: The headteacher (A) made a strong impression (B) on the visiting inspectors, (C) who praised the school for (D) doing a remarkable effort to raise attendance.
options: doing a remarkable effort to raise attendance
items.correction: making a remarkable effort to raise attendance
items.explanation: Effort collocates with make, not do: you make an effort, just as you make an attempt or make progress.

items.q: After the merger (A) fell through, the two technology firms (B) went back to (C) competing fiercely to one another (D) for the same customers.
items.explanation: The verb compete takes with (or against) before a rival and for before the prize; compete to is not a possible pattern.
